title: Daredevil
subtitle: Miller to Zdarsky · main-line Marvel continuity
blurb: The five runs that make up the modern character — Miller, Bendis, Brubaker, Waid, Zdarsky — in the order they were published, with the lead-ins that explain how each one starts.
notes: One continuity, one man, no reboots.

This is main-line Marvel — Earth-616 — from end to end. Matt Murdock's book has run more or less continuously since 1964 and nothing on this list is an alternate universe, a retelling or a restart of the character. The series itself restarts its numbering constantly; the story does not.

Tier 1 is the five runs, and it is most of the list, which is the point: they hand over to each other with nothing missing in between. Tier 2 is three shorter stretches around them — the two lead-ins that explain how a run opens, and Miller's origin miniseries. Tier 3 is the two stretches by other writers that sit between runs — good comics, skippable here. The minimum viable path is Tier 1 alone.

The book has relaunched at #1 six times, so every row names its series by launch year — Daredevil (1964), (1998), (2011), (2014), (2016), (2019), (2022). Two of those relaunches also reverted to the original numbering partway through, which is why #119 is followed by #500 and #28 by #595.
A note says what an issue is — a creator's first or last, a fill-in, a renumbering, where an arc opens — and never what happens in it. Stars mark the issues that matter more than their note suggests.
Links sit on the section headers.
Each section links the Marvel Database page for every series it draws from; those pages list each issue with its credits and cover date. Rows carry no links of their own.

Every issue number, on-sale date, cover date and creator credit read from the Marvel Database (marvel.fandom.com) through its API and cached in tools/data/daredevil.json, header links included. The run boundaries are derived from those printed credits by the generator, which refuses to build if a range is not exactly the writer it claims, or if any section falls out of publication order.

sections.title: Miller arrives
sections.sub: 1979–1980 · he draws it before he writes it
sections.intro: Frank Miller's first stretch on Daredevil is as the artist only, mostly over Roger McKenzie's scripts — two of the ten are written by other hands, and both rows say so. He picks up a shared writing credit near the end of it and the book outright straight after. Skippable, but this is where the look starts.

items.note: Miller's first issue on the book, as artist only.
A fill-in: Michael Fleisher and Steve Ditko.
His first co-writing credit.
David Michelinie writes it, with Miller sharing the credit.

sections.title: Miller & Janson
sections.intro: The run everything after it is measured against. Miller writes all of it and draws most of it, handing the pencils to his inker Klaus Janson for six issues near the end, and the book turns from a superhero comic into a crime one.

items.note: He takes the writing too, and brings Elektra with him.
Klaus Janson pencils as well as inks, through #190.
Miller back on pencils, and the last issue of the first stint.

sections.title: Badlands and Born Again
sections.intro: Miller comes back twice: once for a single issue drawn by John Buscema, then for the seven-issue story that most people mean when they say his Daredevil. David Mazzucchelli draws that one, from the handover issue on.

items.note: A one-off drawn by John Buscema, written two years after he left.
Co-plotted with Denny O'Neil — the handover issue.
Born Again begins, with David Mazzucchelli.
His last issue of the 1964 series.

sections.title: The Man Without Fear
sections.intro: Miller and John Romita Jr. go back to the beginning, seven years after Born Again. It sits here in publication order and reads fine anywhere.

items.note: Miller and John Romita Jr. on the origin.

sections.title: Marvel Knights
sections.intro: Kevin Smith and Joe Quesada restart the book at #1 for Marvel Knights, then David Mack takes the writing. This is the setup the next run opens on, which is the only reason it is here.

items.note: Kevin Smith and Joe Quesada relaunch the book under Marvel Knights.
David Mack takes over as writer.
A fill-in by Jimmy Palmiotti and Joe Quesada.

sections.title: Wake Up
sections.intro: Four issues drawn by David Mack, told from outside the costume. It stands alone and it is the on-ramp.

items.note: Bendis's first Daredevil, drawn by David Mack.

sections.title: Bendis & Maleev
sections.intro: The longest single Daredevil run there is, and the one that set the tone for everything since: procedural, claustrophobic and shot in Alex Maleev's photographic murk. Two fill-in stretches by other writers are marked optional where they fall.

items.note: Six issues by Bob Gale before Bendis returns.
Bendis and Alex Maleev begin the run proper.
Five issues by David Mack, between Bendis's two halves.
Bendis and Maleev resume.
Bendis's last issue.

sections.title: Brubaker & Lark
sections.intro: Ed Brubaker and Michael Lark start on the page after Bendis stops, keep the crime-comic register, and hand the title back to its original numbering at the end.

items.note: Brubaker and Michael Lark start on the next page.
Legacy numbering returns, and Brubaker signs off.

sections.title: Diggle and Shadowland
sections.sub: 2009–2011 · the stretch the next run is a reaction to
sections.intro: Andy Diggle's run, the crossover it builds to and the bridge out of it, interleaved in the order they went on sale. Genuinely optional — Waid's first issue explains where things stand without it — but it is the reason his run looks the way it does.

items.note: Andy Diggle takes over.
The crossover Waid's run is written against.
A four-issue bridge before the relaunch.

sections.title: Waid, Rivera & Martin
sections.intro: Mark Waid restarts at #1 and takes the book back into daylight: bright, buoyant, and drawn by Paolo Rivera and Marcos Martin before Chris Samnee settles in as the regular artist.

items.note: Waid, Paolo Rivera and Marcos Martin restart at #1.
A standalone .1 issue.
Chris Samnee's first issue.
The series restarts at a new #1 next month.

sections.title: Waid & Samnee in San Francisco
sections.intro: The same run, renumbered and relocated. Read it straight on from the section above.

items.note: Same creators, new numbering, new city.
An anniversary special: a Waid lead story and two shorts.
Reprints the four-part Road Warrior digital prelude.
A standalone .1 issue.
Waid's last issue.

sections.title: Soule & Garney
sections.intro: Charles Soule's run, drawn first by Ron Garney. Optional in the same way Diggle's is: the next run opens cleanly without it, and reads a little sharper with it.

items.note: Charles Soule and Ron Garney.
Legacy numbering returns again.

sections.title: Zdarsky & Checchetto
sections.intro: Chip Zdarsky and Marco Checchetto take the crime-comic version of the book and push it as far as it goes. Reads as one continuous story from here to the end of the list.

items.note: Zdarsky and Marco Checchetto begin.
The run pauses here for the event below.

sections.title: Devil's Reign
sections.intro: Zdarsky's run continues as a Marvel event and a companion miniseries, interleaved here in the order they went on sale.

items.note: A line-wide event written out of this run.
A companion miniseries, read between the event's chapters.

sections.title: The Red Fist Saga
sections.intro: One more renumbering, one continuous story, and the end of the run.

items.note: The run picks straight back up at a new #1.
The end of Zdarsky's Daredevil.
